_comment: Economic calendar. Regenerated on a schedule and committed; the site only renders it. Times are UTC and only UTC — the renderer converts to the reader's own clock. See tools/econ-calendar.md.

banks.expect: Hiked 25bp on 16 Sep, 12–0. Cook and Barkin added to the hawkish chorus on Monday; trackers put 28 Oct at roughly 68–72% and at least one more by December at about 94%. UBS notes the Fed has not hiked at an October meeting before an election since 1990

Second hike of 2026 on 10 Sep. Lagarde told the European Parliament on Monday the ECB will take measured steps; the euro fell to a three-month low. Friday's flash HICP is seen 3.6% after 3.2%, and no meeting is ruled out
Held 6–3 on 17 Sep. Bailey said on Friday that high energy prices make the hold harder to maintain and the Bank cannot wait for full evidence; about 80% priced for a November hike

Hiked to 1.25% on 18 Sep, a 31-year high. Tokyo and Washington have spent a week warning on the yen — Trump to Takaichi, Katayama with Bessent, Mimura on Monday — and the pair is 157.35 with 160 treated as the line
Held for a seventh meeting. Minutes flag oil pass-through; about 59% priced for an October hike

Hiked 25bp to 4.60% on 29 Sep, unanimous — the fourth rise of 2026 and the highest since 2011 — and said further tightening may be needed. Markets price another by February; August CPI prints Wednesday
Held at 0% on 24 Sep and nudged the inflation forecast up to 0.7–0.8% on energy. A weaker franc is doing what a hike would; December is the next meeting

events.note: Spoke overnight, a week before the 29 September decision that markets have at roughly 90% for a hike from 4.35%.
Spoke Tuesday, a day before the flash PMIs. No change to the message: no meeting is ruled out, October included.
Up from a revised 16,750. Small, but in the direction the Fed speakers were already pointing. The monthly ADP print is 30 September.

A miss: −2 against 5 expected and 4 before. One regional survey, and the Philadelphia and Kansas City readings this month were firmer — but it is the only activity number this week that has come in below zero.
Defended the September hike at the Treasury Market Conference and gave no guidance on the next move — the Warsh-era pattern.
Spoke on discount-window upgrades and financial stability. Nothing on the rate path.

Supported the September hike and flagged "an increased likelihood of future scenarios in which inflation remains notably above 2%", arguing for a "somewhat more restrictive" funds rate. The dollar index went to its session high on the remarks.

"Will additional hikes be required, and how many? We'll see." Said more than 60% of the PCE basket was rising faster than 3% in July, that "passing" shocks are not proving short-lived, and that the economy is if anything firming. A 2027 voter.

The highest two-year stop since May 2024, 58bp above August's. Demand held — bid-to-cover 2.63 against a 2.61 six-auction average, a 0.2bp tail — so the market took the paper; it just charged more for it. Five-years today, seven-years Thursday.

Reported: housing revenue down 20% on 19% fewer deliveries, average price $473,000, and the first year-on-year rise in backlog in four years. Full-year guidance held at 10,500–11,000 homes. A read on what 7% mortgage rates do to volume rather than price.
A touch under the 54.5 expected, still expanding. Input costs rose at the fastest rate in four months on fuel and energy.
Well above the 50 expected and a seven-month high, ending five months of contraction. Germany's composite went to 53.8 from 51.8.
Exactly as forecast and unchanged on the month. The surprise was in services.
53.0 against 51.7 expected; the composite rose to 53.1 from 52.0. An ECB that has hiked twice this year and ruled no meeting out now has an activity number that agrees with it.
52.0 against 51.4 expected and 51.7 before — the one UK line that improved.
51.7 against 52.0 expected and 52.5 before; the composite slipped to 51.7. The UK was the soft print in a strong day for PMIs, and sterling fell below 1.33.
A small-business payroll read that lands a week before the September jobs report.

57.0 against 53.5 expected and 53.9 before, a 52-month high — after every regional Fed survey this month had pointed the other way. New orders rose to 57.3 and output to 56.7. Input prices across the survey jumped to 66.4, the highest since October 2022.

58.7 against 56.0 expected and 56.5 before, a 59-month high; the composite went to 58.4, the highest since July 2021. S&P Global's Williamson said the survey is consistent with growth of about 5% annualised. The ten-year rose 14.6bp on the day, its largest move since April 2025, and October hike odds went to 73%.

Said "further policy adjustments are likely to be needed" to return inflation to 2% in time, that the Fed had been "out of position", and that inflation risks have risen while labour-market risks have receded. A Governor, so a voter — the first one to say more is coming.

A 3.0 million barrel commercial build against a 0.7 million draw expected, after the API's 1.8 million build. Gasoline and distillate stocks both fell. Crude rose anyway, on Iran rather than on inventories.

The highest five-year stop since June 2006, about 3bp above where the issue was trading at the deadline. Bid-to-cover 2.21 against a 2.33 six-auction average; dealers were left with 15.8%, the most since 2024. The five-year yield closed above 5% for the first time since 2007. Seven-years today.
Nearly double the 20,000 expected, after a revised −15,900 in July. Strong enough to keep Monday's RBA hike at about 90% priced even with the jobless rate ticking up.
4.6% against 4.5% expected — more people looking, not fewer jobs, given the employment gain alongside it.

Held at zero as expected. Inflation is 0.8% and the forecast was nudged up to 0.7% for 2026 and 0.8% for 2027–28 on energy, still inside the 0–2% band. The statement dropped its "increased willingness to intervene" line for a plainer "willing to be active", and the franc weakened on it.

Told a London forum it is "reasonable" to expect another hike this year, that the era of explicit forward guidance is over, and that "the data have not suddenly changed on us". A voter. The third of three voters that day to lean toward more.
197,000 against 201,000 expected, with the prior week revised to 198,000 and the four-week average at 202,250. Nothing in the claims data argues against the hike the Fed's speakers keep describing.
Discretionary spending with a fuel bill attached. Traffic is the line to read.

Cleveland, a voter: the inflation outlook is "highly uncertain" with risks to the upside, and "the longer that high inflation persists, the more challenging and costly it can be to bring it back down".

Philadelphia, a voter who had favoured holding before September: "some modest further tightening may be warranted". Underlying inflation is running 2.5–3% and "the best I can say about it this year is that it hasn't gotten worse".

684,000 against 620,000 expected, with July revised up to 643,000. A strong print a week after mortgage rates went back above 7% — builders are buying the rate down, and the volume is showing up before the margin cost does.
Up 6.4% after a July now revised to −4.3% from −10.5%.

The highest seven-year stop since the tenor was reintroduced in 2009, 57bp above August's and 0.7bp above the when-issued level. Bid-to-cover 2.42 against a 2.50 ten-auction average; indirect bidders took 57.2%, the least since November 2025. The ten-year went through 5.2% after the result. Treasury's buyback the same afternoon filled only $4.1bn of a $6bn cap.
At the Treasury Market Conference, on the morning of a $69bn two-year auction. The venue is the point.
Non-defence capital goods ex-aircraft rose 1.6% against 0.5% expected, and July was revised up from flat to +0.6%. The business-investment line is not slowing.
Flat against −0.4% expected, after July was revised up to +0.9%. Ex-transport rose 0.3% against 0.6%.
Confirmed at 4.6%, up from 4.0% in August. This is the number that took the ten-year to 5.228% on Friday morning before oil fell and pulled it back.

Revised up from the 47.8 preliminary and above 47.6 expected, but down from 51.7 in August and the lowest in four months. The survey director blamed fuel prices and trade frictions for a sharp fall in near-term business expectations.
The only US release of the day. The regional surveys have run hot since the flash PMI printed 57.0; Dallas is the oil-patch one.
On quantitative tightening, three days after Bailey said high energy prices make the hold harder to maintain. About 80% is priced for a November hike.
Richmond. Said last week that inflation pressures may persist for a while; the first Fed voice since Friday's Michigan expectations print and the weekend's oil move.
The first look at trading and banking revenue through the quarter the Fed turned.

Hiked 25bp to 4.60%, unanimous — the fourth rise of 2026, a full point this year and the highest cash rate since 2011. The statement said upside risks to inflation are materialising and further tightening may be needed. AUD barely moved at $0.702; markets price another hike by February.
After a unanimous hike with hawkish guidance already in the statement, the question is whether Bullock leaves November open. Wednesday's August CPI, seen 4.0%, matters more than the press conference.
Second appearance in two days. On Monday she signalled measured steps against inflation and the euro fell to a three-month low near $1.137; Friday's flash HICP is seen 3.6%.

events.event: US FHFA house price index (Jul, m/m)

events.note: Seen 7.23 million after 7.27 million, a second monthly fall; openings have missed consensus two months running. The first labour print of a week that ends with payrolls.
August's 89.4 was the lowest since January and consensus has a third straight fall. Michigan's one-year inflation expectation already jumped to 4.6% on Friday.
Banking supervision, not policy. Listed so the six-speaker day reads in order.

The economic outlook at the Detroit Economic Club. Barr said last Wednesday that further hikes are likely needed and the Fed had been out of position; the first chance to hear whether a 5.24% ten-year changes that.
A 2027 voter. Warsh has stopped giving forward guidance, so between meetings the speeches are the only read on the path.
St Louis, a voter this year, on the US economy — the fourth of six Fed speakers on Tuesday, between Goolsbee at 17:00 and Williams at 18:00 UTC.
Third appearance in a week. Said on Thursday that another hike this year is reasonable and that forward guidance is over.
Payment systems. The sixth and last Fed speaker of the day.
Seen 4.0% after 3.5%, the morning after the RBA hiked to 4.60% and said more may be needed. This print decides whether November is priced as a certainty or a probability.
3.6% in July, above the 2–3% band. Prints the morning after the RBA decides, alongside a headline CPI seen at 4.1%.
Has been below 50 for months. China is the one large economy not fighting inflation.
A final estimate, so a revision is the only way it moves anything.
2.9% last month. The harmonised measure is seen 3.2% after 2.9%; Germany prints two days before the euro-area flash and usually sets the direction of the surprise.
38,000 last month. It correlates with payrolls badly enough that it trades as its own event two days before them.
A final read of a 1.5% second estimate; the PCE rows printing at the same minute are what the market trades.
Seen unchanged at 3.7% with the monthly at +0.4% after +0.2% on the energy pass-through.

events.event: US core PCE price index (Aug, m/m)
US core PCE price index (Aug, y/y)
events.note: The Fed's preferred measure, seen 3.4% after 3.3% — moving away from 2%, not towards it. The Fed named this print when it hiked on 16 September; it lands on quarter-end with October about 65% priced.
Said on Monday that inflation pressures will persist for months and that AI productivity gains will not offset them this year.
A 2027 voter. Warsh has stopped giving forward guidance, so between meetings the speeches are the only read on the path.
The semiconductor print of the fortnight, and the one that can move the Nasdaq on its own.
Minneapolis, after the close on quarter-end day and after the PCE print. The eighth Fed speaker in the fortnight since the hike; the Chair is still not one of them.
22 last quarter. The Bank of Japan has just hiked to a 31-year high, so corporate confidence is now a policy input.
0.8% last month. The SNB held at 0% on 24 September and nudged its forecast up to 0.7–0.8% on energy; a print above that is the only thing that moves a bank with no room to cut.
The only large euro-area manufacturing sector comfortably above 50. It is also the one most exposed to the energy bill.
The final read of the flash 57.0 that moved the ten-year 14.6bp on 23 September. Revisions to flash PMIs are usually small; this one will be read closely anyway.
54.6 last month. Read it with the prices-paid sub-index below rather than on its own.
71.1 last month. This is the cleanest monthly read on whether the energy shock is reaching factory-gate costs.
The Vice Chair, who has said little since the hike. With Warsh silent between meetings, Jefferson is the closest thing to the centre of the committee that speaks.
New York, the day before payrolls. Fourth appearance in eight days.
Freight and input costs in a quarter when heating oil rose 56% over three months.
The capital's print leads the national one by three weeks. At 1.9% headline and 2.0% core it is the one G7 inflation rate still near target, which is why the BoJ is at 1.25% and the yen is at 157.
Seen 3.6% after 3.2%, against a 2% target; core seen 2.5% after 2.4%. Lagarde has promised measured steps; this is the print that decides whether 29 October is one of them.

events.event: Euro area core HICP, flash (Sep, y/y)

events.note: 3.1% last month. Wages are the channel that turns an energy shock into the persistent inflation the Fed says it is hiking against.

Consensus has drifted down to about 84,000 from 100,000 a week ago, after 162,000 in August; Barclays is at 50,000 and expects August revised lower. The first payrolls since the Fed restarted hiking, and the one number this week that could take October away.
Lands ninety minutes after payrolls, which is why nobody trades it.
The larger half of the economy and the one the Fed has been pointing at. Services has stayed above 55 while manufacturing has drifted.
Above 70 for months. This is where the oil move shows up in the data, with a lag of about two prints.

The consumption side of a euro area the ECB has now hiked twice this year. July grew 0.6% year on year, which is the sort of number that lets a central bank keep tightening without being accused of breaking anything.
The first auction of the October cycle. Last month's stop was 4.474%; the two-year sells today at a front end that has moved 50bp in a month.
The first ten-year sale since the yield touched 5%. Last month stopped at 4.834%.

The record of the first hike since 2023 — the meeting that was 12–0 on the vote and 16 of 18 on at least one more this year. With Warsh giving no guidance in public, the minutes are the closest thing to a forward view the Fed publishes.
The record of the 10 September hike, three weeks before the 29 October decision.
The long bond at a yield the market has not paid since 2007. Last month's stop was 5.308%.
The Bank of Canada is still at 2.25% with an October hike about 59% priced. A jobless rate at 6.4% is the argument against; oil pass-through is the argument for.
The first big airline of the season, reporting into jet fuel that has doubled in a year. Guidance on fuel and demand is the read, not the quarter.
The first October survey. September's preliminary was 47.8 with one-year inflation expectations at 4.6%; the expectations line is the one the Fed reads.

events.event: Columbus Day — US bond market closed
events.note: Equities trade; Treasuries and the banks do not. The IMF and World Bank annual meetings run in Washington through the week.
The record of the meeting that markets have at about 90% for a hike from 4.35%. How close the vote was, and what August's 4.6% unemployment did to it, is the read.
The final read of the flash due 30 September. Germany sits at 2.9% against a euro-area 3.2%, and the ECB has said no meeting is ruled out.

The start of the third-quarter reporting season, with Goldman Sachs, Wells Fargo, Citigroup and BlackRock the same morning. FactSet has S&P 500 earnings growing about 29% for the quarter, a third straight quarter above 25%; the banks report into a curve at 5% and a financials sector that is flat on the year.

events.event: Johnson & Johnson and UnitedHealth Q3 earnings

events.note: The first full month of sales agreed at mortgage rates above 7%. August fell 2.0%.
Pushed back a week by the Golden Week holiday. Still under 1% while the US prints 3%-plus; the gap is the whole US–China rates and currency story.
3.4% in August with the monthly at +0.4%. The first CPI after the September hike, two weeks before the 28 October decision.
0.3% last month. The Fed is hiking against the risk that energy leaks into core; this is where it would show.
The anecdotal survey two weeks before the 28 October meeting. The September hike was justified partly on regional reports of pass-through; this is where that gets updated.
August's +39,500 against 20,000 expected is what tipped the RBA into a September hike. Unemployment was 4.6%; UBS thinks it needs to reach about 5% to bring inflation back.
4.6% last month, headline 5.4%. Pipeline pressure the Fed has been pointing at.
August rose 1.2% with the control group up 1.4%. Nominal sales are being flattered by fuel prices; the control group strips that out.
4.3% in the second quarter. The one large economy still not fighting inflation reports the morning after a fortnight of holiday-thinned data.
3.0% in August against a 2% target with core at 2.4%. The Bank of Canada has held at 2.25% for seven meetings and has an October hike about 59% priced; this lands ten days before it decides.

howToRead.title: Impact is about how much price moves, not how much the number matters
howToRead.text: A high-impact release is one where the spread widens, liquidity thins and the first move often reverses. That is a statement about market structure at 08:30, not about economics. Plenty of important data is marked medium because the market has already priced it.

howToRead.title: The forecast is the level that matters, not the previous
howToRead.text: Price reacts to the gap between actual and forecast, not to whether a number went up or down. A 5.3% PPI print against a 5.3% forecast is a non-event; the same print against a 4.7% forecast is not.

howToRead.title: Two releases at the same minute are one event
howToRead.text: Agencies batch their releases, so you will often see three or four rows sharing a print time — jobless claims alongside the Philadelphia Fed, import prices alongside retail sales. Nobody trades the smaller one on a morning like that. When you see the same time twice, read the highest-impact row and ignore the others.

howToRead.title: A release-driven wick is not displacement
howToRead.text: Models built on liquidity runs misfire badly on data prints, because the move has no intent behind it — it is an auction gap. If your playbook has no rule about scheduled releases, this page is the argument for adding one.
